summary: This work demonstrates wireless excitation of a superconducting microwave resonator at 20 mK inside a dilution refrigerator, comparing performance against a wired reference at $f_r = 10.8$ GHz using a TX/RX pair with double split-ring resonator metalenses. Direct comparison reveals that wireless excitation preserves intrinsic resonator properties ($Q_i$, $f_r$, temperature-dependent frequency shift from quasiparticles) but exhibits an additional loss channel with $|\Delta Q_L| \approx 650$ arising from stray radiation coupling through unintended pathways within the reflective cryostat cavity.
motivation: Scaling quantum computers to thousands of qubits requires reducing the dense network of interconnects between cryogenic processors and room-temperature electronics, which introduce substantial thermal loading and routing congestion in dilution refrigerators.
method: The authors built a wireless link operating at $\sim$10.6 GHz through a 10 cm diameter aperture between the 4 K and 20 mK stages, using matched TX and RX modules with metalens beam-shaping, and systematically compared wired and wireless excitation of a NbN resonator using cryogenic switches to isolate propagation pathways.
result: At $T_{mxc} = 20$ mK, wireless transmission preserves resonator $Q_i$ and frequency evolution across 20 mK–3 K, but introduces $\approx$650 additional losses in $Q_L$ due to parasitic coupling; RF absorbers suppress cavity reverberation but do not eliminate residual stray excitation with estimated parasitic capacitance $C_p \sim 40$ fF.
